entry.title: Texas And LSU Had A Barnburner Of Dumbass Football
entry.summary: The Texas Longhorns triumphed in an exciting, last-second 22-21 victory over the LSU Tigers on Saturday, thanks to a heroic effort by QB Arch Manning and some typical breaking down of the LSU defense. But if you did not watch the contest in full, do not let the thrilling end fool you: This was some of the year's dumbest football, authored by two of our dumbest college football programs. Let's start with the six interceptions total in this game: three for each, which is nice and neat. At first, it was LSU's Sam Leavitt throwing most of the picks, two in the first half, which makes it particularly strange that LSU was leading for the majority of this game. They were helped by the fact that Manning tossed two picks in the second half, to add to one he threw in the second quarter, and as a result the game was the Tigers' for the taking—21-10 late in the third, and still 21-16 when they punted with only 2:19 to go. But if nothing else, Manning has shown an ability to get better when his back is against the wall. And if you're going to beat Texas, you have to stomp them out completely. Despite Manning's overall pedestrian performance, 174 yards on 19-of-35 passes, his night climaxed with the crucial touchdown. In the game's final two minutes, Manning led a 12-play, 58-yard drive down the field, culminating in a seven-yard run on third down at LSU's 11-yard-line and then a four-yard TD pass to RB Raleek Brown for the go-ahead score. Cue the Texas sideline going absolutely, understandably nuts.

entry.title: Irreal: Vim To Emacs
entry.summary:
journey from Vim to Emacs. Actually, his journey was from Nano to Emacs by way of Vim. When he first started using Linux, Nano was the default editor and he began with that. Eventually he wanted more power and because Vim seemed more popular in the forums he inhabited, he learned Vim. He really like it and the power that it brought him was an eyeopener.
He experimented with other Vim-like implementations but they didn’t work for him so he stuck with Vim. Eventually he tried Emacs and almost immediately became a convert. Like me, he jumped right in and didn’t try to use Evil or some other Vim emulation. Like many of us, he loved the experience and now wants to do as much as he can in Emacs.
As always, a lot of the action is in the comments. Many said that immigrants from Vim should use Evil because it gives you the best of both worlds: the modal, composable editing commands of Vim and the power and flexibility of Emacs. Others said that Evil induces a sort of cognitive dissonance where neither system is fully in control.
There is, of course, the occasional post proclaiming loudly that Emacs is no good because it uses Lisp with all those parentheses. The ankle biting aside, the comments offer an intelligent and useful commentary on Sahkopi4’s journey.

entry.title: Irreal: Setting The Timezone In Emacs
entry.summary:
hint for those of you who travel and phone home with Emacs. Here’s the situation: you are travelling and log into your home server with SSH and emacsclient. It’s wonderful. Just like being at home except the date/time stamp is wrong. The time and date are whatever your home server thinks they are but you want them to be local time.
The answer is simple. You simply need to change the TZ (timezone) environment variable to reflect your current location. For example, if you’ve travelled to New York (in the US) you would set TZ to “America/New_York”. Emacs, of course, provides a command to do this: (setenv "TZ" "America/New_York").
The zone codes can be a bit opaque so Choi has added a command to the latest Casual suite to set the TZ variable complete with completion. Take a look at his post if you’re interested.

entry.title: Charles Choi: Setting the Timezone in Emacs
entry.summary:
Here’s the problem: You are traveling in a different time zone from the Emacs server instance you are accessing remotely via ssh + emacsclient. All clock calculations in that Emacs session are using the local timezone relative to where the server is located. But what you really want is emacsclient to use the current timezone you are in, so things like the mode line clock render accordingly. To adjust the timezone in an Emacs session, use the command setenv to set the environment variable TZ with a timezone defined in the zoneinfo database. This can be called from Elisp as shown below.
1
(setenv "TZ" "Asia/Seoul")
The latest v3.1.0 update of Casual adds the command casual-timezone-set-tz that provides a completion interface for selecting a timezone to pass to setenv.
1
M-x casual-timezone-set-tz RET
Note that setting TZ impacts the Emacs session globally; any other running behavior depending on a clock should be taken into account.

In order to see the note, you'll need to press C-c C-c a second time to complete the capture. Then org-capture adds the item into the Org file, along with the note.
My preference in this situation is to write only the first phrase or sentence of the note. Then I issue the two presses of C-c C-c and complete the note at its destination. entry.title: Irreal: Journelly 1.5
entry.summary:
the release of Journelly 1.5. It’s the formal release of the beta version that I recently wrote about. I can’t say enough about this release. As I’ve said before, my Journelly database is over 4 thousand entries long and before this release Journelly was getting laggy and hard to use but this release resolved all those problems. Now Journelly is as snappy as it was when I had only a few entries and everything about it seems faster and easier.
But wait. There’s more. Ramírez has added an “on this day” feature as well as adding features that make searching for entries by date easier.
If you use Journelly as a journal, you may be interested in the new “on this day” feature. There’s a new button that will show you entries happening on the same day from other years. My particular use case for Journelly is as a memo book so I have no use for this feature. Fortunately, the new Journelly makes it easy to toggle it off if you don’t want it.
The other new significant feature is enhanced searching by date. In the search function you can use on: keyword with several different date formats to search for entries with a particular date. There’s also a calendar button that lets you choose the date from a calendar presentation if you prefer.
You may wonder why I have this entry tagged emacs. I consider Journelly intrinsically linked with Emacs because Journelly keeps its database in an Org file and that means that I can use Emacs and Org mode to search and edit that database. That doesn’t seem like much but I find myself doing it all the time. Journelly has become integrated into my Emacs workflow and become an important part of it.
In the mean time, those of you not in the Journelly beta program now have access to these updates. I can’t speak for Ramírez, of course, but if you’d like to be in the beta program, email Ramírez. He’ll probably be glad to add you.

entry.title: Charles Choi: Announcing Burnish
entry.summary: Org mode is often celebrated for its ability to “write once, export anywhere.” With such power comes added complexity: Exporting a file requires the user to typically go through a multi-step process (e.g. C-c C-e <some char> <some other char>). If the user is concerned with previewing changes to their file, then another step of viewing the exported output is required. Having to do this repeatedly gets tedious fast. Such is the motivation for Burnish. Burnish is a new Elisp package I’ve made to automate the export and viewing of an Org file. It provides an Emacs minor mode (burnish-mode) that when enabled, does the following upon save of an Org file: Export the Org file to a specified export backend. View the exported output in another Emacs window or by external tool. Most all of the default backends provided by Org mode are supported by Burnish. That said, Burnish is highly configurable, allowing for users to define for themselves the export and view workflow for existing or third party backends. Read the Burnish User Guide to learn more about it. As it is new, feedback is always welcome. If you really find it useful, please show your gratitude by buying me a coffee. Burnish v1.0 is now available on MELPA.

entry.title: Lars Ingebrigtsen: OK, OK, I’ll just use tmdb
entry.summary:
After last night’s post, I realised I was probably just getting too invested in somehow using imdb for the “who’s that actor, anyway?” command for my Emacs-based video player. Not only is it an extremely fragile setup that’s gonna stop working, but it’s also very slow — it takes half a minute to return the actor profile images. So I just implemented a tmdb API shim and then I ask it for the actor profile photo instead. tmdb doesn’t have as large a data base, but… The API is free (for non-commercial use) and is extremely easy to use. Things are now faster:
The main wait is from the response from the LLM — I’m using gemini-3.8-flash. I’ve tried gemini-3.1-flash-lite, and it’s much faster… but gives the wrong result most of the time. No, that’s not Roy Scheider, Gemini! So now the setup is less Rube Goldberguesque. Sort of: I hit a key on my li’l wireless keyboard.
It’s picked up by a Python script that listens for evdev events.
It uses emacsclient to notify the Emacs running on the TV machine.
Emacs there tells mpv to do a screenshot.
Emacs waits until the screenshot arrives on disc.
Emacs sends it to Gemini and says “who dis? JSON please”.
Gemini responds and Emacs then creates an SVG overlay with the actor name.
rsvg-convert converts to PNG and then imagemagick convert to BGRA.
Emacs asks mpv to display it.
Emacs asks tmdb for the actor profile URL and fetches the image.
If it gets a response, it then recreates the svg with the image embedded.
(repeat 8-9).
Couldn’t be simpler.

entry.title: Irreal: BYOK
entry.summary:
interesting post about BYOK. BYOK is a “writer deck”, a device exclusively for writing that has no distracting apps or even a connection to the Internet. The idea is that writers can’t get distracted when they reach a temporary block by escaping to social media or something similar; they have to push through the block and get on with their writing.
According to Martin, BYOK is better than most devices in its class but there are still problems. He doesn’t like the available fonts and the screen—as you can see from the picture in his post—is pretty small, about 6 lines depending on the font. That seems to me to amount to a rather uncomfortable working environment. Fortunately, I don’t usually find myself distracted when I’m writing.
Then there’s the matter of research. Very often you need to look something up when you’re writing and you can’t do that with something like BYOK so you need to switch devices, pulling you even further out of the flow. And as Martin observes, it’s not easy to integrate your notes either.
The deal buster for me, though, is the builtin editor. It’s not Emacs based and doesn’t even support Emacs keybindings for navigation. As I’ve repeatedly said—as recently as yesterday—I simply can’t comfortably write outside of Emacs anymore. Martin is a relative newcomer to Emacs but he’s already feeling the discomfort. Once the Emacs way sets in, he’ll be just like me and won’t consider doing serious writing outside of Emacs.
Even if I were subject to being distracted by the greater Internet, I would simply turn off my WiFi to produce what is effectively an Emacs based writer deck. One thing for sure, I’m not giving up Emacs and suffering a second rate writing environment.

entry.title: Irreal: Why Use A Word Processor When You Have Org?
entry.summary:
And now it’s all this, Dr Drang has a post on using TextEdit versus using Pages. He’s a Mac user, obviously, but that doesn’t matter so much. The real argument is over whether one should use a word processor or some sort of text based editor.
There can be no doubt on where I stand on the issue. The only time I can remember using a “word processor” of any type in the last 3 decades was when I had to collaborate on another author’s file as a technical editor1. As I’ve said before, whenever I write in anything other than Emacs, I feel like I’m in Bizarro World where nothing works as it should. That includes even things like iMessage which is why I tend to use emacs-everywhere for it and most other things.
Dr Drang is nominally the same. He says he almost never uses a Word Processor but sometimes for a one-off he thinks it makes sense to use a word processor rather than one of his LaTeX or Markdown templates. That seems backwards to me. Sure, maybe you don’t want to use a template for a technical report to write a quick note to your baby sitter but Pages or any other word processor is not the simple alternative. I’d simply use Org and export it to whatever format seems appropriate. Even if Dr Drang is not an Emacs user, he is a Markdown user so surely the easy thing for him to do is to dash off his quick note in Markdown.
Really, unless you have collaboration issues, there’s no reason to subject yourself to the horrors of a word processor.
Footnotes: 1
That post was so long ago that I was still using Groff instead of Org to typeset documents. I’ve done technical editing since then that also required a Word clone and the experience was no better.
